where: Section 1, paragraph beginning "At β = 0 the closed-loop poles..."
problem: It says that in a two-pole amplifier the closed-loop poles cross into the right half plane for too much β. A loop with only two poles can never become unstable: under negative feedback the two poles meet on the real axis, break away and stay in the left half plane for every value of β. This also contradicts Section 3 of the same chapter, which says a two-pole loop is always made safe by phase margin, and it contradicts worked example 1, where the gain margin is infinite.
fix: Say: "Increasing β moves them. In a two-pole amplifier the closed-loop poles become complex and ring more as β rises, but they never cross the imaginary axis. With three or more poles they can cross into the right half plane when β is too large. That movement is the stability question."

problem: The answer treats the 1 kHz pole as giving a full −90° at 5 kHz. The pole is only a factor of 5 below the crossover, so it gives −arctan(5) = −78.7°, not −90°. The stated phase −116.6° and PM 63.4° are therefore both wrong. The chapter's own exam trap warns against exactly this −90° shortcut.
"Deliberate positive feedback that makes T = 1" can be read as a statement about magnitude only, which would be wrong; an oscillator needs unity magnitude and zero phase around the loop.
fix: "Deliberate positive feedback with |T| = 1 and ∠T = 0° is the oscillator case in 4.4."
